analysis.one_liner: Bans foreign-owned companies and foreign-funded groups from spending in US elections and tightens foreign-agent registration rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: referred to two House committees in July 2021, sent to a subcommittee on November 1, 2022, and left to die when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tighten the existing ban on foreign money in US elections. It would treat corporations with meaningful foreign ownership — 5% if a foreign government owns the shares, 20% for other foreign owners — as foreign nationals, who are already barred from campaign spending. It would bar foreign-affiliated nonprofit 'dark money' groups from funding super PACs or attack ads, stop political committees from taking money raised by registered foreign agents, and overhaul the Foreign Agents Registration Act: ending a loophole for lobbyists, letting the Justice Department demand documents during investigations, setting fines, and creating a dedicated enforcement unit. The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who want to know who is paying for political ads and influence campaigns. Ordinary citizens' votes would face less competition from money traceable to foreign governments or foreign-owned companies, and disclosures under the Foreign Agents Registration Act would become more complete and searchable.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters wanting foreign money out of elections

how_it_helps.text: Corporations at least 5% owned or controlled by a foreign government, or 20% owned by other foreign nationals, would be treated as foreign nationals under the campaign-spend ban, closing a route by which foreign money reaches US elections through domestic companies.

Nonprofit 501(c)(4) groups receiving 5% of their funds from foreign governments (or 20% from foreign nationals generally) could no longer give to super PACs, make independent expenditures, or pay for electioneering ads, closing a 'dark money' channel for foreign-linked cash.

Political committees could not accept direct or bundled contributions from people registered as foreign agents, and foreign nationals could not help decide how election money is spent or fund state and local ballot initiative campaigns.

The bill repeals the exemption that let lobbyists registered under US lobbying law avoid registering as foreign agents, lets the Attorney General issue civil investigative demands to gather evidence, sets civil fines up to $200,000 for knowing violations, and creates a dedicated Justice Department unit — funded at $10 million a year — to enforce the Foreign Agents Registration Act.

analysis.who_pays: Foreign-owned corporations and foreign-invested companies that would lose the ability to fund US election activity; lobbying and public-relations firms representing foreign principals, who would face registration, fees, and fines; and foreign-funded 501(c)(4) groups that would lose access to super PACs and issue ads.

drawbacks.text: The ownership thresholds would rely on stock ownership: a company listed on US exchanges with sizable foreign shareholding would be treated as a foreign national even if its operations and management are entirely American, which critics say could sweep in large swaths of the US corporate sector and chill legitimate corporate political speech.

Fines for late or incomplete registration statements would apply 'without regard to the state of mind of the person' — up to $10,000 per violation for a late filing — a strict-liability penalty that honest filers could trip over.
Platforms with 50 million or more monthly US users would have to keep foreign-agent disclosure labels attached to posts even after they are shared, a compliance requirement that platforms would bear.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core aim — keeping foreign government money out of US elections — is widely shared and addresses a real gap, since foreign money can currently reach campaigns through partially foreign-owned companies and foreign-funded nonprofits. The main design risk is overbreadth: using raw stock-ownership percentages means globally traded US companies and mutual-fund-adjacent structures could be swept in, and the strict-liability fines are blunt. A carefully drafted version would have narrowed the ownership tests; the bill as written trades some overreach for a simpler, harder-to-evade rule.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee its whole life — referred to the Judiciary and House Administration committees, then sent to a Judiciary subcommittee about a year in, and it never got a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Katie Porter introduced the bill on July 29, 2021, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Administration Committee.
Six Democratic colleagues cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

On November 1, 2022 — more than a year after introduction and two months before the Congress ended — it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, where no further action followed.
Neither committee ever held a markup, and the House never voted on the bill; it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The channels the bill would have closed stay open: foreign-owned corporations, foreign-funded 501(c)(4) groups, and lobbyists for foreign principals operate under the same rules as before, and no one had to register, pay a fee, or disclose anything new.

industries.industry: Foreign-agent lobbying and public relations firms
industries.note: The bill would end their exemption from registering as foreign agents, require fees and stricter filings, expose them to fines up to $200,000, and bar them from raising money for political committees. Their business is influencing US politics for foreign clients, which the bill would make more visible and more expensive.

Companies 5% owned by a foreign government or 20% owned by other foreign nationals would lose the ability to fund US election activity through corporate treasuries. The bill's premise is that their spending conflicts with the interest of US voters in elections free of foreign money.

Groups taking 5% of receipts from foreign governments or 20% from foreign nationals could no longer fund super PACs, independent expenditures, or electioneering ads, cutting off an undisclosed route for foreign-linked money into campaigns.

Platforms with 50 million or more US monthly users would have to keep foreign-agent disclosure labels attached to posts even after sharing, a real compliance cost — but a narrow one, and the bill also extends some transparency to online political propaganda.
